title: Activities of Nonideal Solutions
lead: Real solutions stray from ideal behavior. Activity keeps the ideal formula for the chemical potential and moves the departure into an activity coefficient, here for dissolved salts, for a solvent on Raoult's scale and a solute on Henry's, and for solutes too involatile to measure directly.
notes: The page prints no credit; the ions' Gibbs function stays printed as the book writes it, one substitution per line.
exercise_notes: The one exercise and its solution are AI-written; numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance, and its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI.

exercises.source_id: suggested a means of calculating the mean activity coefficients from experimental data
exercises.prompt:
A solution of MgCl₂ in water at 298.15 K has a molality of 0.010 mol/kg. Take the dielectric constant of water as 78.54.

  1. What is the ionic strength $\kIion$ of the solution?
  2. What is the mean activity coefficient $\kgammapm$ from the Debye-Hückel law, $\log_{10}\kgammapm = -\dfrac{1.824\times10^6}{(\kepsilon\kT)^{3/2}}|\kzplus\kzminus|\sqrt{\kIion}$?

parts.hint: Each formula unit gives one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻.
Work out the constant for water at 298.15 K first.

footnotes.html: The exponent is $1/(x+y)$. For MX, with $x = y = 1$, it gives the square root above.

The limiting law has a minus sign and the product of the charges: $\log_{10}\kgammapm = -\dfrac{1.824\times10^6}{(\kepsilon\kT)^{3/2}}|\kzplus\kzminus|\sqrt{\kIion}$. So $\kgammapm$ is below 1 and falls as the ionic strength grows.

The sentence breaks off here. For water at 25 °C ($\kepsilon = 78.54$, $\kT = 298.15$ K) the constant $1.824\times10^6/(\kepsilon\kT)^{3/2}$ is 0.509, so $\log_{10}\kgammapm = -0.509\,|\kzplus\kzminus|\sqrt{\kIion}$.
The line should read $\ln a_1 = \ln \kxone \approx -\kxtwo$: at low solute concentrations $a_1 \approx \kxone = 1 - \kxtwo$, and $\ln(1-\kxtwo) \approx -\kxtwo$ for small $\kxtwo$.
